subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: setting a specific measurable target [Thinking]
passage: Monday night. “Get fitter” has never worked for me. It's too soft; I can always say I'm fitter than yesterday without doing anything. So I wrote real numbers on the inside of my diary cover. Goal: run 5 km without stopping at the school race on 14 December. Now: I can run 1 km before I have to walk. Plan: lengthen each week's run by roughly a quarter of a kilometre. Parveen ma'am checked it after PE and said it was the first time a student had written a date and a starting distance. It felt a little silly, then a little exciting, because for the first time I could tell exactly how far away 5 km was. — Sarika

qa.a: One kilometre, before having to walk.

qa.q: How does Sarika feel about the written plan?
qa.a: A little silly at first, then excited and hopeful, because the numbers show exactly how far the goal is.

qa.q: What else could Sarika do to keep going, and why?
qa.a: Write down each run's distance in the diary, since seeing the small gains builds confidence on tired days.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Parveen ma'am?
qa.a: Parveen ma'am sees a student who set a date and a starting point, which makes the goal specific and easier to coach.

grounding: A teen writes a date, a starting distance and a weekly increase for a 5 km run.

qa.a: Pooja feels determined but knows "get fit" is vague; a clear goal and date make progress something to track and feel proud of.

qa.q: What else could Pooja add to make the plan safer?

grounding: Shows a teen setting a clear running target with a race date, a one-kilometre start, and small weekly increases.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: setting a specific measurable target [Thinking]
passage:
In Irawati's village outside Nashik, the school's inter-house race was set for Republic Day: five kilometres along the canal road. She had never run further than the bus stop.
That night, under the kitchen bulb, she opened a fresh notebook page. “Get fit” was useless, she thought; you can't tick off “get fit”. So she wrote: Goal: run 5 km without stopping. Date: 26 January. Now: 1 km, from the temple to the second culvert.
She counted the weeks on the calendar: eleven. “If I add a little every week, just to the next marker stone, I'll get there with time to spare.”
Her friend Alka read the page over her shoulder. “Marker stones?”
“The canal has one every half kilometre. They're my plan.”
The next morning at six, Irawati ran to the second culvert, and stopped, exactly as written.

qa.q: What did Irawati write as her starting distance?
qa.a: 1 km, from the temple to the second culvert.

qa.q: Why did Irawati think "get fit" was useless?
qa.a: She felt it gave nothing to aim at or tick off, and a measurable goal made her feel more confident about getting there.

qa.q: What else could help Irawati stick to the plan on hard mornings?
qa.a: Running with Alka on some days, so someone expects her at six and the marker stones feel less lonely.

qa.q: How might Alka see the marker-stone plan?
qa.a: Alka may be amused at first, then impressed that the stones turn a big goal into small, visible steps.

grounding: Shows a teen writing a race date, a starting distance of one kilometre and a plan to add a little each week toward running five kilometres.
